title: Overview and justification
body:
This short course is about practice- and work-based learning: learning by doing real tasks in real or realistic settings. By the end you will be able to explain what it is, recognise the many forms it takes across different subjects, and describe the benefits it offers you.

In many disciplines you will be expected to take part in practice or work-based learning at some point in your degree. Knowing what it is, and why it matters, helps you recognise it when it comes and make the most of the chance.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain what practice- and work-based learning is
recognise the range of forms it takes across disciplines
describe the benefits of practice- and work-based learning for your development.

title: In real academic practice
body: Practice- and work-based learning is becoming a central part of higher education, as more courses build links with industry and professional practice. Whatever you study, there is a good chance you will meet it, as a placement, fieldwork, a live project or something similar. Understanding it now means you can recognise the opportunity and get more from it later.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, what learning by doing is: what practice- and work-based learning means. Second, the many forms it takes: how it looks across different subjects. Third, the benefits to you: why it is worth doing. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

The examples and activities in this course use invented people, organisations and placements to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, employer or source you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: At university, a lot of learning happens by reading, listening in lectures, and writing. Practice- and work-based learning is different: you learn by doing real tasks, often in a real or realistic setting. This lesson looks at what that means, so you can recognise this kind of learning and say what makes it distinct.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are early in your studies, and you may not have done a placement or a work-based project yet. You are not expected to have any workplace experience. The aim here is simply to understand what practice- and work-based learning is, so you know what to expect when it arrives.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain that practice- and work-based learning means learning through doing real tasks in a real or realistic setting
recognise practice- and work-based learning in a worked example of a student's experience
identify what makes an activity practice- or work-based learning, rather than classroom study, in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Practice- and work-based learning is learning that happens through doing. Instead of only reading about how something is done, you do it yourself, in a workplace or in a task built to work like one. The experience itself, that is, the actions you take and what happens as a result, is where the learning comes from.

It covers a wide range of activities across many different subjects, from a placement in an organisation to a practical project set inside your course. What they share is simple: you learn by taking part in real or realistic work, not only by studying it from the outside.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a time you learned something by doing it, rather than by reading or being told. What did doing it teach you that you could not have got from a book?

title: Summary
body: Practice- and work-based learning is learning that happens through doing: taking part in real tasks, in a workplace or a work-like setting, rather than only studying them from the outside. You can now explain what it is and recognise it in a student's experience. The next lesson looks at the many forms it takes across different subjects.

title: Orientation
body: In the last lesson you saw that practice- and work-based learning means learning by doing. This lesson shows how many different shapes that takes. A placement in a hospital, fieldwork on a coastline, a live brief from a real client: all are learning by doing, and they look very different from one subject to the next.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Practice- and work-based learning covers a broad range of activities, relevant to an equally wide set of disciplines. It is not one thing. In some subjects it means a placement in an organisation; in others it means fieldwork, a studio or laboratory project, a live brief from a real client, volunteering, or a realistic simulation set inside the course.

What ties them together is that each puts you into real or realistic work. The form changes with the subject, but the idea stays the same: you learn by taking part. Knowing the range helps you recognise this kind of learning whatever shape it takes in your own course.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of your own subject. What form of learning by doing does it include, or could it include: a placement, fieldwork, a studio or lab project, a live brief, or something else?

title: Summary
body: Practice- and work-based learning takes many forms across different subjects: placements, fieldwork, studio and laboratory projects, live projects, volunteering and simulations. You can now recognise that range and give an example in a named discipline. What they share is learning by doing. The next lesson turns to why this kind of learning is so valuable to you.

title: Orientation
body: You have seen what practice- and work-based learning is, and the many forms it takes. This lesson asks why it is worth doing. Learning by taking part in real work gives you things a lecture cannot: authentic experience, skills that employers value, and a clearer sense of the kind of work you are heading into.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not expected to have gained these benefits yet. The aim is to understand what practice- and work-based learning offers, so that when the chance comes you can see what is in it for you and begin to make the most of it.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: describe the main benefits of practice- and work-based learning for your development
recognise a benefit of practice- and work-based learning in a worked example
identify a benefit you could gain from a practice- or work-based activity in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
The first thing to say about practice- and work-based learning is that it offers authentic, real-world experience. It opens up the workplace you intend to move into as a graduate, so you learn what the work is actually like, not only what books say about it.

From that flow several benefits. You build practical skills by using them, not just by reading about them. You grow in confidence as you handle real tasks. You start to see yourself as a future professional, and you gain experience that employers value when they choose who to hire. In short, the experience develops you, not just your knowledge.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Imagine you finish a placement or project in your subject. What is one thing you would hope to come away with: a skill, more confidence, or a clearer sense of your direction?

title: Summary
body: Practice- and work-based learning is valuable because it offers authentic experience of the real workplace, builds practical skills by using them, grows your confidence, and helps you see yourself as a future professional. You can now describe these benefits and recognise them in a student's experience. With a clear picture of what this learning is, the forms it takes and why it matters, you are ready to make the most of it when it comes.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Practice- and work-based learning is no longer a vague phrase: it is learning by doing, and you know what it offers. You can explain what it is: taking part in real tasks, in a workplace or a work-like setting, rather than only studying them from the outside. You can recognise the many forms it takes, from placements and fieldwork to live projects and volunteering. And you can describe its benefits: authentic experience, practical skills, growing confidence, and a clearer sense of the professional you are becoming. Look back at the confidence check to see how far you have moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, practice- and work-based learning is something you can look out for across your degree. When a module offers a placement, fieldwork or a live project, you will know what it is and what it can give you. It is also what employers value: real experience, used skills, and someone who has already seen the workplace from the inside.

title: Where this goes next
body: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the intermediate course looks at how to make the most of a placement or project, and the advanced course turns to reflecting on experience with Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle. Going wider: Reflective Practice, Understanding Learning, Assessment and Feedback, and Academic Writing all put this kind of learning to work.

title: Explore the concept
instruction: Select the card to reveal the definition, an example and related terms.
definition: Learning that happens through doing real tasks, in a workplace or in a task built to work like one.
extendedDefinition: Instead of only studying how something is done, you take part in doing it, and the experience itself is where the learning comes from. It covers a wide range of activities across many different subjects.
example: A nursing student on a hospital placement, or a design student working on a brief for a real client, is learning in this way.

body:
Consider two students on the same course, both told their module includes a work placement.

{{learner-a}} treats the placement as time away from real study. {{learner-a}} turns up, follows instructions, and waits to be told what to do, expecting the real learning to happen later, back in lectures. The days pass and tasks get done, but {{learner-a}} does not see the placement itself as learning.

{{learner-b}} treats the placement as the learning. {{learner-b}} takes on real tasks, watches how experienced people work, and notices what the setting teaches that a textbook cannot. The work is not a break from study; it is a different way of studying, through doing.

Both students did the same placement. Only {{learner-b}} recognised it as practice- and work-based learning: learning that comes from taking part in real work.
title: Worked example
Spotting learning by doing
body: Use these questions to tell practice- and work-based learning apart from classroom study. Try them on your next module.
instruction: Tick each item once you have thought it through.

_items.text: Am I doing a real task, rather than only reading or hearing about it?
Is the setting a workplace, or a task built to work like one?
Is the experience itself meant to teach me something?
Would I learn this differently if I only studied it from the outside?
Am I taking part in the work, not just observing from a distance?
Can I name what the doing is teaching me that a lecture could not?

title: Formative check: what learning by doing is
displayTitle: Which statement best describes what practice- and work-based learning is?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which statement best describes what practice- and work-based learning is?

_items.text: Learning that happens through doing real tasks, often in a real or realistic setting.
_items.feedback: Yes. Practice- and work-based learning comes from taking part in real work.

_items.text: Reading about a profession in detail before you ever try it.
_items.feedback: Reading about work is useful study, but it is not learning through doing.

_items.text: Memorising the steps of a task so you can repeat them in an exam.
_items.feedback: Memorising steps is classroom study, not learning by taking part.

_items.text: Watching a documentary about an industry you might join.
_items.feedback: Watching from the outside is not taking part in the work itself.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Practice- and work-based learning is learning by doing real tasks in a real or realistic setting.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about doing real tasks, rather than reading, memorising or watching.
_incorrect.final: Practice- and work-based learning means doing real tasks in a real or realistic setting. Reading, memorising and watching are all studying it from the outside.

title: Formative check: recognising learning by doing
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's placement practice- and work-based learning?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's placement practice- and work-based learning?

_items.text: They took part in real tasks and treated the experience itself as the learning.
_items.feedback: Yes. Taking part in real work, and learning from it, is what makes it practice- and work-based learning.

_items.text: They waited until they were back in lectures to do the real learning.
_items.feedback: That treats the placement as a break from study, not as learning in itself.

_items.text: They spent longer on the placement than the first student.
_items.feedback: Length of time is not what makes it learning by doing.

_items.text: They read more about the organisation before they started.
_items.feedback: Reading beforehand is preparation, not learning through the work itself.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student took part in real tasks and treated the experience as learning.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student DID, beyond turning up or reading.
_incorrect.final: The placement was practice- and work-based learning because the student took part in real tasks and learned from the experience itself.

title: Explore the concept
body: Review each card to see a different form of practice- and work-based learning, and the subjects where it is common.
instruction: Read through the cards below.

_items.title: Placements
_items.subtitle: In an organisation
_items.text: You spend time working inside a real organisation, taking on tasks alongside its staff. Common in health, business, education and social work.

_items.title: Fieldwork
_items.subtitle: Out in the field
_items.text: You gather data or practise skills in a real setting outside the classroom, such as a coastline, an archive or a community. Common in geography, biology and history.

_items.title: Studio and laboratory projects
_items.subtitle: Inside the course
_items.text: You produce real work in a studio or lab that mirrors professional practice, such as a design, a performance or an experiment. Common in art, engineering and the sciences.

_items.title: Live projects and volunteering
_items.subtitle: Real briefs, real people
_items.text: You take on a real brief from a client or community, or volunteer with an organisation, and your work has real consequences. Common across many subjects.

body:
Two students on different courses are each offered a piece of learning by doing.

{{learner-a}} is told the activity is 'just fieldwork' and assumes it does not really count, because it is not a proper placement in an office. {{learner-a}} almost turns it down, thinking practice- and work-based learning only means one thing.

{{learner-b}} recognises their own live project for a real client as the same kind of learning, in a different form. It is not a placement, but it is real work with real consequences, so it is learning by doing, shaped to fit their subject.

Both were offered practice- and work-based learning. Only {{learner-b}} saw that it comes in many forms, and that fieldwork and a live project both count.

title: Formative check: matching the form
displayTitle: In {{context}}, you spend several weeks working inside a real organisation, taking on its tasks. Which form of practice- and work-based learning is this?

_items.text: A placement.

_items.feedback: Fieldwork gathers data or practises skills out in the field, not inside one organisation's daily work.

_items.text: A simulation.
_items.feedback: A simulation imitates real work; here the work is real, inside an actual organisation.

_items.text: A lecture.
_items.feedback: A lecture is classroom study; this is learning by doing.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Working inside a real organisation on its tasks is a placement.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which form means working inside a real organisation on its own tasks.
_incorrect.final: Working inside a real organisation, taking on its tasks, is a placement. Fieldwork, simulations and lectures are different things.

body:
Two students finish the same work placement and are asked what they got out of it.

{{learner-a}} says it was fine, but cannot point to anything gained. {{learner-a}} did the tasks without noticing what they taught, and comes away with hours completed but no sense of having developed.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option where you take part in real work.

body: Which statement about the forms practice- and work-based learning takes is correct?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which statement about the forms practice- and work-based learning takes is correct?

_items.text: It takes many forms across subjects, such as placements, fieldwork, projects and volunteering.
_items.feedback: Yes. It takes many forms across disciplines.

_items.text: It always means a placement in an office.
_items.feedback: A placement is one form, not the only one.

_items.text: It is one fixed activity, the same in every subject.
_items.feedback: It is a broad range of activities.

_items.text: It happens only in health and business degrees.
_items.feedback: It appears across a very wide set of subjects.

_feedback.correct: That's right. It takes many forms across disciplines.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how many different shapes this learning can take.

body: A geography student gathers data on a coastline as part of their course. Which form of practice- and work-based learning is this?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A geography student gathers data on a coastline. Which form is this?

_items.text: Fieldwork.
_items.feedback: Yes. Gathering data in a real setting outside the classroom is fieldwork.

_items.text: A placement in an office.
_items.feedback: A placement means working inside an organisation, not gathering data in the field.

_items.text: A written exam.
_items.feedback: An exam is classroom study, not learning by doing.

_items.text: A lecture.
_items.feedback: A lecture describes the work; this student is doing it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Gathering data out in a real setting is fieldwork.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which form means working out in the field, away from the classroom?

body: Which of these is a benefit of practice- and work-based learning described in the course?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is a benefit of practice- and work-based learning described in the course?

_items.text: Authentic, real-world experience that opens up the workplace you are heading into.
_items.feedback: Yes. Authentic experience of the real workplace is a key benefit.

_items.text: A guarantee of higher exam marks.
_items.feedback: It develops you; it is not a promise of exam marks.

_items.text: A way to avoid the workplace until after graduation.
_items.feedback: It opens up the workplace while you study, rather than avoiding it.

_items.text: Less work than any classroom module.
_items.feedback: It is a different, valuable kind of learning, not less work.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Authentic, real-world experience is a core benefit.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the benefit about authentic experience of the real workplace.

body: A student finishes a placement able to name new skills, more confidence and a clearer career direction. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student finishes a placement able to name new skills and direction. What does this show?

_items.text: That the experience developed them, which is a benefit of practice- and work-based learning.
_items.feedback: Yes. Being able to name what you gained shows the experience developed you.

_items.text: That the placement was too easy.
_items.feedback: Naming what you gained is not a sign the placement was easy.

_items.text: That they completed enough hours.
_items.feedback: Hours completed do not show development.

_items.text: That classroom study is no longer needed.
_items.feedback: It develops you alongside your studies; it does not replace them.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The student was developed by the experience, which is a benefit of this learning.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What does being able to name skills, confidence and direction tell you?

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: what practice- and work-based learning is, the many forms it takes, and the benefits it offers you. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one way of looking at your studies.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to have done a placement or project yet. The aim is to see these three ideas as one. Then you can spot learning by doing when it comes, and be ready to take it up across the rest of your studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: recognise how what practice- and work-based learning is, the forms it takes and its benefits connect as one way of looking out for learning by doing
recognise learning by doing at work in a student's experience across a course
plan how you will look out for and take up learning by doing in your {{context}} study

title: Concept: definition
body: Looking out for learning by doing is a single habit built from three ideas. When a chance to learn by doing appears, you recognise what it is, place the form it takes, and see what it could give you. The three ideas from the earlier lessons are the parts of that one habit.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, looking out for learning by doing becomes part of how you read your course. Each time a module offers a placement, fieldwork or a project, you pause and name it, work out its form, and ask what it could give you. Over a degree, that habit means you spot chances others walk past.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of one subject or module you will study soon. Where might a chance to learn by doing appear in it, and how would you recognise and take up that chance?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Learning by doing is most useful when you look out for it across your whole degree. You bring the three ideas together: you recognise a chance, place its form, and see what it offers, then take it up. It is that habit, not any single placement, that shapes the graduate you become.

title: The steps as one process
body: Looking out for learning by doing is one practice you work through each time a chance appears, not three separate skills. Select each step to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each step.

_items.title: Notice a chance
_items.body: Notice a chance to learn by doing in your course, such as a placement, fieldwork or a live project.

_items.title: Name it
_items.body: Name what it is: learning through doing real tasks, not only studying them from the outside.

_items.title: Work it out
_items.body: Work out which form it takes, and what it could give you.

_items.title: Take it up
_items.body: Decide to take it up, ready to learn from the experience itself.

_diagram.title: Looking out for learning by doing

title: Worked example
body: Two students start the same course, both told it includes a placement and a live project later on. One treats each as a box to tick and signs up without thinking about what it is. The other names both as learning by doing, works out what form each takes, and sees the skills and experience they could gain. By the end, the second student has chosen chances that build towards the work they want.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to look out for learning by doing
body: Use these questions whenever a module offers a chance to learn by doing.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Can I see a chance to learn by doing in this part of my course?
Can I name it as learning through doing real tasks, not only studying them?
Can I say which form it takes, such as a placement, fieldwork or a project?
Can I name what it could give me, such as skills, confidence or experience?
Am I ready to take it up and learn from the experience itself?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat these three ideas as one practice rather than three separate facts?
body: Why is it more useful to treat these three ideas as one practice rather than three separate facts?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat these three ideas as one practice rather than three separate facts?

_items.text: Because together they let you spot a chance to learn by doing, place its form, and see what it offers, all at once.
_items.feedback: Yes. As one practice, the three ideas work together each time a chance appears.

_items.text: Because knowing what it is on its own is enough, so the forms and benefits do not matter.
_items.feedback: Each idea helps, but it is the three together that let you recognise and take up a chance.

_items.text: Because treating them as one means you never have to learn the forms it takes.
_items.feedback: The forms are part of the one practice, not something it lets you skip.

_items.text: Because one practice is quicker to memorise than three separate ideas.
_items.feedback: It is not about memorising. The three work together when a real chance appears.

_feedback.correct: That's right. As one practice, the three ideas work together whenever a chance to learn by doing comes along.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what you gain by using the three ideas together, not one at a time.

displayTitle: A student spots a live project in their course, names it as learning by doing, sees it could build real skills, and signs up. What does this show?
body: A student spots a live project in their course, names it as learning by doing, sees it could build real skills, and signs up. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student spots a live project in their course, names it as learning by doing, sees it could build real skills, and signs up. What does this show?

_items.text: They brought the three ideas together as one practice: they recognised the chance, placed its form, and saw what it offered.
_items.feedback: Yes. Naming it, placing its form and seeing its benefit is the one practice at work.

_items.text: They skipped straight to signing up without knowing what the project was.
_items.feedback: They did name it as learning by doing first. That is part of the practice.

_items.text: They treated the project as ordinary classroom study.
_items.feedback: They saw it as learning by doing, which is the opposite of ordinary classroom study.

_items.text: They only looked at the benefits and ignored what the project actually was.
_items.feedback: They named it and placed its form too, not only its benefits.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Recognising the chance, placing its form and seeing what it offers is the practice working as one.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at the three things the student did before signing up.

displayTitle: You want to look out for learning by doing in {{context}} this year. Which plan best brings the three ideas together as one practice?
body: You want to look out for learning by doing in {{context}} this year. Which plan best brings the three ideas together as one practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to look out for learning by doing in your subject this year. Which plan best brings the three ideas together as one practice?

_items.text: When a chance appears in {{context}}, name what it is, work out its form, see what it offers, and take it up.
_items.feedback: Yes. That uses the three ideas together each time a chance to learn by doing comes up in {{context}}.

_items.text: Wait until your final year, then read about placements in {{context}} without taking one.
_items.feedback: Reading about it is not taking part. Learning by doing means doing the work.

_items.text: Only consider a chance in {{context}} if it is a formal placement in an office.
_items.feedback: A placement is one form. Fieldwork, projects and volunteering count too.

_items.text: Sign up to anything in {{context}} without thinking about what it is or what it offers.
_items.feedback: Recognising what it is and what it offers is part of the practice, not a step to skip.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Naming it, placing its form, seeing its benefit and taking it up uses all three ideas in {{context}}.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the plan that brings all three ideas together in {{context}}.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: Which description best fits bringing the three ideas together as one practice?
body: Which description best fits bringing the three ideas together as one practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which description best fits bringing the three ideas together as one practice?

_items.text: Spotting a chance to learn by doing, naming its form, seeing what it offers, and taking it up.
_items.feedback: Correct.

_items.text: Learning only the definition and ignoring the forms and benefits.
_items.feedback: The three ideas work together, not alone.

_items.text: Waiting for a placement and turning down every other form.
_items.feedback: Learning by doing takes many forms, not only placements.

_items.text: Reading about work experience instead of taking part in it.
_items.feedback: Learning by doing means doing the work, not only reading about it.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: A student notices fieldwork in their course, names it as learning by doing, sees it will build real skills, and takes it on. Which parts of the practice has the student used?
body: A student notices fieldwork in their course, names it as learning by doing, sees it will build real skills, and takes it on. Which parts of the practice has the student used?

ariaQuestion: A student notices fieldwork in their course, names it as learning by doing, sees it will build real skills, and takes it on. Which parts of the practice has the student used?

_items.text: Recognising what it is, placing its form, seeing what it offers, and taking it up.
